newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S., South Korea link aid to North with talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., South Korea link aid to North with talks.

text.p: The United States and South Korea have agreed that any large-scale food or economic aid to North Korea must wait until Pyongyang joins proposed four-nation peace talks, Seoul officials said on Thursday.

The agreement was reached during talks in Seoul this week with Charles Kartman, acting assistant secretary at the U.S. State Department, said Lee Yong-joon, head of the South Korean foreign ministry's U.S. department.
Kartman left for China on Wednesday for bilateral talks.
North Korea has demanded substantial food aid as a condition for joining peace talks involving the two Koreas, the United State and China.
The talks are aimed at securing a lasting peace to replace an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

"We confirmed our stand that no preconditions be attached to the peace talks," Lee told Reuters. "Food aid and economic measures will be allowed during the talks if North Korea takes steps to ease tensions on the Korean peninsula."

A foreign ministry official, who asked not to be identified, said U.S. officials told North Korea in a meeting in New York last week that Washington would not ease economic sanctions until Pyongyang agreed to the talks.
The United States and South Korea have said, however, they would continue to take part in international relief programmes on humanitarian grounds.
South Korea has pledged $6 million and the United States $10 million to a United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) appeal for the Stalinist state.
WFP Executive Director Catherine Bertini arrived in Seoul on Thursday for a three-day visit to appeal to Seoul to increase its contribution.
The programme, saying recent inspections found the potential for starvation "on a massive scale" in North Korea, wants to double its appeal to 200,000 tonnes of food.
A vessel headed for North Korea on Thursday, carrying more than $1 million worth of food and vegetable seed donated by South Korean religious and civic groups.
